metaDescription: Ward County minerals near Monahans span decades-old vertical wells and new Delaware Basin horizontals. Get a valuation that accounts for both.
heroLead: Ward County, home to Monahans, has some of the oldest continuously producing acreage in the Permian sitting right alongside newer horizontal development, and knowing which one your family's minerals fall under changes everything about what they're worth.
intro: Monahans has been an oil town since long before the Delaware Basin horizontal boom, and Ward County carries that history in its title records — leases from the 1930s and 1940s, held by production for decades on shallow vertical wells that still pump a few barrels a day. That's one layer of ownership here.

The other layer is newer: Wolfcamp horizontal development pushing in from the more active parts of the Delaware Basin to the south and west, picking up acreage that had been quiet for years. If your family's minerals sit in Ward County, I'll tell you plainly which layer you're in — and whether recent permitting has changed the picture on ground that used to be considered tapped out.

sections.heading: Monahans and the county's deep production history
paragraphs: Monahans sits close to some of the earliest developed acreage in this part of the Permian, and a lot of Ward County's mineral title reflects that — leases that have been held by production continuously since well before most current owners were born. Those older vertical wells produce modestly now, but the leases themselves are often still active, which matters if a new operator wants to redrill the same acreage horizontally.

The Monahans Sandhills, the dune field the town is named near, sits over part of this legacy production and remains largely undeveloped surface even where the minerals below have been leased and drilled for generations.

sections.heading: Where new Delaware Basin horizontals are reaching into Ward County
paragraphs: Operators active in the busier parts of the Delaware Basin to the south, around Reeves and Loving counties, have steadily extended horizontal development north and east into parts of Ward County. That's changed the calculus for owners whose minerals sat under old, low-producing vertical wells for decades — some of that acreage is now getting a second look for horizontal Wolfcamp development.
If you haven't checked on your Ward County interest in a while, it's worth confirming whether any new permits have gone in nearby before assuming nothing's changed.

sections.heading: Old leases, new operators
paragraphs: It's common in Ward County to find a mineral deed and lease from decades ago still technically controlling the acreage, even though the operator currently producing it isn't the same company that signed the original lease. Leases and working interests here have changed hands many times over the decades through mergers, sales, and assignments, and your division order should reflect whoever's currently paying — but the underlying lease terms can still trace back to a document your grandparents signed.
That layered history is normal for a county this old in oil terms, and it's exactly the kind of thing a careful title review sorts out before anyone quotes you a fair number.

sections.heading: Courthouse records in Monahans
paragraphs: The Ward County clerk's office holds records stretching back nearly a century in places, which is both a blessing and a challenge — deep history means more documentation to work through, but also more opportunity for gaps: unrecorded assignments, probate that never got filed, name changes across generations. None of that is unusual here.
Bring whatever you have, even something as old as an original 1940s lease, and we'll do the work of tracing it forward to confirm current ownership before closing.

faqs.question: My family's Ward County lease is from the 1940s. Is it still valid?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, if it's been continuously held by production, which is common in this county. Old leases don't expire just because they're old, as long as production has continued without a lapse. We verify this through Ward County clerk records before valuing your interest.

faqs.question: Is Ward County seeing any new drilling, or is it all old wells?
faqs.answer: Both. There's deep legacy vertical production around Monahans, and newer Wolfcamp horizontal development has been extending in from the more active Delaware Basin counties to the south. We check current permits near your specific tract rather than assuming based on the county's older reputation.

faqs.question: The operator on my check isn't the company my grandparents originally leased to. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: No, that's normal. Leases and operating interests in Ward County have changed hands many times over the decades. As long as your division order reflects the current operator and your interest is accurately calculated, the change of hands doesn't affect your ownership.

faqs.question: How does the Monahans Sandhills area affect drilling or mineral value nearby?
faqs.answer: The dune field itself is mostly undeveloped surface, but the minerals beneath and around it have been leased and produced for decades. Surface terrain doesn't typically limit horizontal drilling the way it might have limited older vertical operations, so nearby acreage remains in play.

faqs.question: What does closing look like for an older Ward County lease with limited paperwork?
faqs.answer: We start with whatever documents you have and use Ward County clerk records in Monahans to trace the chain of title forward from there. Older leases with gaps take a bit more time to clear, but we handle that work and keep you informed rather than asking you to track it down yourself.
